prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms opened the 10^-18 regime of timekeeping

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: one prize part, B013, to Katori and Ye. The achievement is a single mechanism that can be written down and checked. At the magic wavelength the lattice light shift is the same for both clock states, so thousands of atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime without Stark-shift or Doppler error, and the statistical gain from many atoms is then used without the systematic penalty. That is a new capability, not a refinement of an old one, and it is what separates it from the two precedents the chair asks us to test. The 2005 prize rewarded the frequency comb and laser spectroscopy, which turned optical frequencies into countable ones, and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single trapped ions. A lattice clock uses neither the single-ion route nor a new counting technique; it replaces the one-particle clock by an ensemble clock whose systematics are controlled by a design principle. The meaning is understood, which I weigh heavily: the error budget is built from the physics (blackbody shift, hyperpolarisability, collisions, lattice depth) and has been verified across independent laboratories by direct clock-to-clock comparison, over more than twenty years. The consequences are concrete and measurable: gravitational redshift over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and dark-matter couplings, and the road map to the redefinition of the second. On the question of waiting for the redefinition, the prize honours the discovery, and the discovery is mature now; the redefinition is an application that depends on policy as much as on physics, so I would not make the award conditional on it. I read the round-1 files and nothing in them moved me from this configuration. All eight statements agree on the configuration, which I treat as weak evidence by itself, since the chair is right that agreement can reflect clean attribution as much as scientific weight. My reason is the mechanism and its verification, not the count.
statement.case_against: The objection that carries real weight is attribution within the field. Lemonde, Ludlow, Oates, Takamoto, Bloom, Derevianko and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups made real contributions to accuracy and to the theory of lattice-clock shifts, and I have not independently verified early strontium and ytterbium priority dates. A two-name credit is defensible only if the citation is phrased around the invention (Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium lattice clock) and the realisation of the accuracy frontier (Ye), which limits the claim without pretending nobody else mattered. A second objection is that precision metrology has been honoured many times, so a committee that insists on a new state of matter or a new window on nature will find a clock prize unambitious; I accept that this is a matter of taste, but I do not think it is a scientific defect. Finally, KPZ (B042), where I began, has deeper conceptual reach, but its credit remains hard to settle and almost no colleague supports it, so I do not carry it into a final configuration as a primary.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Katori and Ye are credited for the same achievement or for two separable contributions, and says the prize should reward the original work and not a second group that did it much better.
responses.response: I think this is the right test and B013 passes it, provided the citation says so. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock; Ye drove the same scheme to the accuracy and stability frontier with the many-body strontium clock and showed that the ensemble approach works at 1e-18. These are two stages of one achievement, concept and realisation, rather than a rival and a copy. I would keep the words 'invention and realisation' in the citation so the committee's reasoning is on the record, and I would not try to rank the two contributions against each other. If you can verify priority for the Katori proposal and the first lattice-clock demonstration, that would settle the point.

responses.point: Danielsson describes clocks as useful rather than existential and states that his taste runs toward a new window on nature (B016), while accepting B013 on maturity and checkability.
responses.response: I share part of that taste, which is why I started with KPZ. But I would resist calling the lattice clock merely useful. The clocks are used to measure millimetre-scale redshift and to bound dark-matter couplings, and they probe physics that was not accessible to single-ion clocks, so nature does answer back here. On B016, the attribution is the weakness I raised in round 1: Falcke and Doeleman from a collaboration of hundreds, with the chair arguing that Zensus cannot be omitted, is much less settled than Katori and Ye. I also repeat my correction on Ye and 2005, since the chair summary carries it forward: that prize went to Glauber, Hall and Hänsch, and Ye was a collaborator of Hall, not a laureate. That is an association to weigh, not a prior prize.

responses.point: Pearce observes that broad support may reflect clear attribution rather than scientific weight, argues that the Higgs discovery has greater weight, and keeps B001 or B059 as fallbacks if the Ye precedent is disqualifying.
responses.response: I agree that support counts are not an argument, and I take the Higgs discovery to have the greatest weight on our list. But the question of weight cannot be separated from the question of whom we name: ATLAS and CMS each have several leaders with a comparable claim, and a three-name selection from four candidates leaves one of Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni or Virdee out on judgment that I cannot defend from the physics. A prize whose citation we cannot justify against the omitted people is weaker than a smaller prize whose credit is clear. Since Ye was not a prior laureate, I do not think the 2005 point triggers your fallback. If the committee can agree an attribution for B001 in a way that is not arbitrary, I would reconsider, and I would then want it as a second part, but I have not seen such an agreement.

responses.point: Eriksson wants to know whether magic-angle graphene should wait for the pairing mechanism, and whether a two-part prize pairing a metrology achievement with a condensed-matter one is feasible within three people.
responses.response: On maturity, the continuum model and the flat bands are well tested, but the origin of the superconductivity is unsettled and the credit among Bistritzer-MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Cao and others, plus earlier theory, is still contested, so I would keep B046 as an alternative and not as a primary. On the two-part question, I do not see it as workable: B013 uses two names, so a second part would have only one name left, and B046 needs at least two or three. I would not weaken either part to make that fit, and no round-1 file asks for a second part, so I would keep the single prize.

uncertainties: Early priority dates for strontium and ytterbium lattice clocks (Katori versus Lemonde and others), and whether the committee can verify them before the vote.
Whether colleagues treat the 2005 and 2012 prizes as making a lattice-clock prize incremental, which is a judgment about novelty and cannot be settled by facts alone.
Whether the redefinition of the second, which is still pending, should be seen as part of the case or as irrelevant to the discovery.
Whether the Higgs attribution among ATLAS and CMS leaders can be settled in a way that would justify a different configuration.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I am at the University of Gothenburg, as are committee colleagues Johansson and Olsson at Chalmers in the same local physics environment, with no collaboration with them or with any credited candidate. I have no known connection with Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Kardar, Zhang or Takeuchi, and I report no conflict for B013. I note that B042, my opening first choice, is in my own broad field of non-equilibrium statistical physics, which is a reason for caution in advocating it, and it is only an alternative.
